deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the closing passage of §13 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published posthumously 1867). The section shows how badly behaved a convergent trigonometric series, and the functions attached to it, can be. Ω is the formal trigonometric series under study. F(x) = C' + A_0 x^2/2 - Σ A_n/n^2 is the twice formally integrated series, and the previous page writes C' + A_0 x - Σ (dA_n/dx)/n^2 for its first derivative.

(A) Continuation of the example started on the previous page. Take Φ(q) = Σ_{n≥1} n^{-3} (1-q^n) log(-log(1-q^n)). The logarithms are to be normalised so that they vanish at q=0. Expand Φ in ascending powers of q and put q = e^{ix}. Then Im Φ(e^{ix}) is a trigonometric series G(x).
- Claim 1: the twice-differentiated series G''(x), which plays the role of Ω, converges at infinitely many points of every interval.
- Claim 2: the first difference quotient of G (its first derivative) becomes infinite at infinitely many points of every interval.

Mechanism (my filling-in): put t = 1 - q^n. Near t = 0 the n-th term behaves like t·log(-log t). This is continuous and tends to 0, but its derivative behaves like log(-log t) → +∞ (very slowly).
- t → 0 happens exactly when e^{inx} = 1, i.e. x ∈ 2πZ/n.
- So the derivative blows up on the dense set of x that are rational multiples of 2π.
- The weights n^{-3} keep the series and its second-derivative series under control, so that the latter converges densely.
- The point: Ω may converge densely while the associated function F is too irregular for its first derivative to be integrated over any interval.

(B) Riemann's second claim: in the same extent (densely, infinitely often between any two arguments), a trigonometric series can converge even though its coefficients do not tend to 0. His example is S(x) = Σ_{n≥1} sin(n! x π).

(B1) x = p/q rational: for n ≥ q, n!·x is an integer, so sin(n! x π) = 0. The series is a finite sum and converges.

(B2) Irrational points; all verified by me via Taylor-series remainders.
- x = e: write n!·e = N_n + r_n with N_n = Σ_{k≤n} n!/k! and r_n = Σ_{k>n} n!/k! ≈ 1/(n+1), decreasing.
  - N_n = n·N_{n-1} + 1 with N_0 = 1, so N_n ≡ n+1 (mod 2).
  - Hence sin(n! e π) = (-1)^{n+1} sin(π r_n), an alternating sequence with decreasing modulus: it converges by Leibniz.
  - For x = m·e the term is (-1)^{m(n+1)} sin(mπ r_n). For odd m it still alternates and converges. For even m all terms are eventually positive, ~ mπ/n, and the series diverges. So only odd multiples of e work, as Riemann says.
- x = 2/e: 1/e = Σ (-1)^k/k!, so n!·(2/e) = (even integer) + 2s_n with s_n ≈ (-1)^{n+1}/(n+1).
  - The terms ≈ (-1)^{n+1}·2π/(n+1) alternate, and the same holds for every integer multiple, so all multiples converge.
  - By contrast 1/e itself diverges: the derangement numbers D_n ≡ n+1 (mod 2) cancel the sign alternation.
- x = sin 1 = Σ (-1)^k/(2k+1)!: the integer part I_n of n!·sin 1 is even for even n and odd for odd n.
  - The remainder is ≈ (-1)^{n/2}/(n+1) for even n and O(1/n^2) for odd n.
  - Hence for every integer multiple the terms are a conditionally convergent alternating part plus an absolutely convergent part, so the series converges.
- x = cos 1: the integer part L_n of n!·cos 1 is always odd. The remainder is ≈ ±(alternating in n)/(n+1) for odd n and O(1/n^2) for even n. All multiples converge.
- x = (e - 1/e)/4 = sinh(1)/2: see errors.
errors: Normalisation in example (A): the outer logarithm cannot vanish at q=0 as written. -log(1-q^n) = q^n + q^{2n}/2 + ..., so log(-log(1-q^n)) = n·log q + O(q^n), which is singular at q=0 and has no expansion in ascending powers of q. A natural repair (my suggestion) is log(-log(1-q^n)/q^n). This does vanish at q=0, changes each term only by n^{-3}(1-q^n)·n·log q-type pieces, and does not affect the local behaviour at q^n → 1 that drives the argument.

Claim (A) is stated without proof. That the twice-differentiated series converges densely, and that the derivative is infinite densely, is plausible from the local behaviour t·log(-log t). However, the convergence of the doubly differentiated trigonometric series at the relevant points is not demonstrated.

The value x = (e - 1/e)/4 = sinh(1)/2 appears to be wrong.
- Write n!·sinh 1 = J_n + u_n. For odd n, J_n = Σ_{k≤(n-1)/2} n!/(2k+1)! is odd: the k=(n-1)/2 term is 1 and all others are even. Also u_n = O(1/n^2).
- So n!·x = J_n/2 + u_n/2 has fractional part → 1/2, and sin(n! x π) → ±1 along odd n.
- Numerically: n=5 gives sin(70.512π) ≈ 0.9993; n=7 gives ≈ -1. The series therefore diverges at this point.
- Neighbouring candidates fail too: sinh 1, cosh 1 and cosh(1)/2 all diverge.
- This slip appears to have been carried into the printed text; I am not certain whether it has been noted in the secondary literature.
Minor: the transcription's 'Differenzenquotient' should be 'Differentialquotient' (Riemann writes 'Differenzialquotient').

results.what: Construction of a trigonometric series, Im of the q-expansion of Σ n^{-3}(1-q^n) log(-log(1-q^n)) at q=e^{ix}. Its doubly differentiated series converges densely, yet its first derivative is infinite on a dense set (the rational multiples of 2π).
results.modern_name: Example of a function with densely infinite derivative / pathological trigonometric series (Riemann's §13 examples)

results.what: Σ sin(n! x π) converges at every rational x and at uncountably/infinitely many irrationals (odd multiples of e; multiples of sin 1, cos 1, 2/e), although its coefficients do not tend to 0.
results.modern_name: Riemann's example showing that convergence on a dense set does not force coefficients → 0 (contrast Cantor–Lebesgue theorem, which needs convergence on a set of positive measure / an interval)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1854/1867; the Cantor–Lebesgue theorem is due to Cantor (1870) and Lebesgue

deep.surprise_reason: This page is the draft of the final paragraph of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift §13, which was published in 1867. Both examples, including Σ sin(n!xπ) with the listed irrational points, are well known as Riemann's. The only noteworthy details are two slips: the dubious value (e-1/e)/4 and the q=0 normalisation of the log-log expression.

checkable.sympy: [ (sum(factorial(n)/factorial(k) for k in range(n+1)) - (n+1)) % 2 for n in range(1,15) ]
checkable.asserts: N_n = Σ_{k≤n} n!/k! satisfies N_n ≡ n+1 (mod 2) (all entries 0), giving the alternating signs for x=e.
Terms at x=e alternate in sign and decrease in modulus like π/(n+1), so Σ sin(n! e π) converges.
At x=2e (an even multiple) the terms are positive ~2π/(n+1), so the series diverges, matching 'ungerade Vielfache von e'.
At x=2/e the terms alternate ~(-1)^{n+1}·2π/(n+1), so the series converges.
At x=sin 1 the terms tend to 0, with the even-n terms alternating ~±π/(n+1) and the odd-n terms O(1/n^2).
At x=cos 1 the terms tend to 0 with the alternating pattern ensuring convergence.
At x=(e-1/e)/4 the odd-n terms tend to ±1, so the terms do not tend to 0 and the series diverges (Riemann's claim fails here).
log(-log(1-q)) = log(q) + q/2 + ..., i.e. it is singular at q=0, so the stated normalisation cannot hold literally.
The derivative of the local building block t·log(-log t) tends to +oo as t→0+, which is the source of the densely infinite derivative.

transcription_corrections: In the formula 'Σ_{1}^{∞} sin(n!) xπ', the argument is sin(n! x π); the manuscript has the summation limits written '1,∞' under the Σ.
First line: 'wo die Logarithmen' is an insertion above a struck-out 'log'; the transcription's '{+Logarithmen+} [-...-]' is correct.
